"Jive" as a verb has three distinct meanings in modern English. Knowing all three — plus one important note about a closely related word — will give you the complete picture.
Meaning 1: To be consistent or in agreement with something

This is the most common way "jive" is used as a verb today. When two things jive, they match, fit together, or make sense together. When they don't jive, they contradict or conflict with each other.

Examples:

  • "His story doesn't jive with the facts." → His story conflicts with the facts; they don't match.
  • "What she told me jives with what I already knew." → What she said is consistent with what I already knew — it fits.
  • "Something about his excuse just doesn't jive." → Something feels off or inconsistent about his excuse.
  • "The numbers in your report don't jive with the numbers in mine." → Our numbers contradict each other.

Think of it this way: two puzzle pieces either fit together or they don't. If they fit, they jive. If they clash, they don't jive.

This meaning is used constantly in everyday American English — in conversations, news articles, workplace discussions, and more.
Meaning 2: To talk in a teasing, exaggerated, or misleading way; to kid or fool someone

This is an older, informal/slang sense of "jive." When someone is jiving you, they are teasing you, messing with you, or not being straight with you. They might be exaggerating, being playfully deceptive, or just pulling your leg.

Examples:

  • "Stop jiving me — tell me the truth." → Stop messing around / stop misleading me.
  • "Are you jiving, or is that for real?" → Are you joking/teasing, or do you actually mean it?
  • "He was just jiving — he didn't mean it seriously." → He was just talking loosely/playfully, not being sincere.

You'll hear this less often in contemporary speech than Meaning 1, but it still appears, especially in older literature, films, and among older speakers.

"Jive" is also a style of energetic partner dance associated with swing and early rock and roll music. As a verb, to jive means to perform this dance.

Examples:

  • "They were jiving all night at the party." → They were dancing the jive all night.
  • "Can you jive?" → Do you know how to dance the jive?

This usage is more common in British and Australian English than in American English. In everyday speech, you're more likely to hear this in the context of dancing competitions or music events.

Here is something many learners (and even native speakers) don't know, and getting this right puts you ahead of most people.

There is another word — "jibe" — which is the older, technically "correct" word for Meaning 1 (to be consistent with something). It comes from sailing: when a sail shifts to align with the wind, it jibes — it comes into line. Over time, this sense of "coming into agreement" moved into everyday language.

So technically speaking:

  • "The story doesn't jibe with the facts" is the more traditionally correct phrasing.
  • "The story doesn't jive with the facts" is the version most people actually use today.

Because "jive" (meaning to be consistent) has become so widespread and natural-sounding, most modern dictionaries now accept it fully for this meaning. In casual and everyday speech, "jive" and "jibe" are interchangeable in this sense, and nobody will consider it an error.

However, in formal writing — think academic papers, legal documents, serious journalism — careful writers still prefer "jibe" for the "to be consistent with" meaning, and reserve "jive" for the slang/dance meanings.

Practical advice: In conversation and informal writing, freely use "jive" for all three meanings. In formal writing, use "jibe" when you mean "to be consistent with," and save "jive" for the teasing or dancing senses.
Quick summary of the three meanings

Jive = to be consistent with / to align with
→ "These two accounts just don't jive."

Jive = to tease, mislead, or kid someone
→ "Don't jive me — is it true?"

Jive = to dance the jive
→ "She jived beautifully at the competition."

One final thing worth knowing: in all three meanings, "jive" carries a slightly informal, casual tone. You wouldn't typically hear it in very formal or stiff language. It belongs naturally to everyday speech and writing.
